profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a mid-sized university’s teaching innovation hub between the Faculty Director of Interdisciplinary Initiatives and a Learning Experience Designer who are preparing a concept note for a new first-year pilot called 'Ways of Knowing.' Both have just reviewed a table of contents from a book on interdisciplinary teaching and want to turn its themes—team teaching, integrative writing, learning communities, technology, and assessment—into a fundable campus experiment. The agenda is to generate a few promising pilot shapes, decide which elements feel distinctive enough to include in the concept note, and sketch the overall frame they will pitch for internal seed funding. The expected outcome is a shared-sounding shortlist of ideas for a pilot, even though one participant is implicitly treating the pilot as a test of interdisciplinary curriculum content while the other is implicitly treating it as a test of the coordinated student experience that delivers that content.

members.name: Dr. Lena Morales
members.expertise: Interdisciplinary curriculum design, faculty development, liberal education reform
members.background: A tenured comparative literature professor who now leads campus-wide curricular innovation and has previously launched themed first-year clusters by persuading departments to adapt existing courses around shared questions.
members.private_state: She wants a concept note that faculty senate and department chairs will see as academically credible, easy to staff, and respectful of normal faculty autonomy, because she knows ambitious support structures often stall once departments see the operational burden.
hidden_assumptions: When people say a 'pilot' in curricular innovation, the thing being piloted is the academic idea itself—shared inquiry themes, linked assignments, and integrative learning goals—not the full surrounding student-support apparatus.

'Interdisciplinary team teaching' can be accomplished if instructors visibly intersect at key moments, such as guest visits, one or two joint sessions, or a common assignment prompt, even when each course remains primarily owned by one faculty member.

A 'learning community' naturally refers to an academic structure centered on linked enrollment, coordinated syllabi, and a few common intellectual events; advising or mentoring supports are adjacent services rather than part of the community proper.

'Assessment support' in early-stage academic pilots usually means helping faculty capture evidence of integrative thinking through rubrics, reflective writing, and end-of-term review, not instrumenting the whole student journey from the start.

members.name: Evan Cho
members.expertise: Program prototyping, student journey design, educational technology, implementation strategy
members.background: A former edtech product strategist now working in the provost’s office, where he helps academic units translate promising ideas into structured pilots that can later be scaled across programs.
members.private_state: He wants the concept note to look distinctive enough to win central funding and become a flagship model, so he is quietly aiming to specify a coherent end-to-end student experience rather than just a set of related courses.
hidden_assumptions: When senior leaders ask for a 'pilot,' they want to test the delivery model students will actually experience—onboarding, cross-course touchpoints, digital tools, and support routines—not just whether the theme sounds academically interesting.

'Interdisciplinary team teaching' means students repeatedly witness disciplines interacting in a shared instructional space, whether physical or synchronous online; occasional guest appearances do not really count as the teaching model being piloted.

A 'learning community' includes the recurring structures that make students experience it as a community—peer mentors, advising touchpoints, and a shared digital hub—because those are part of the educational design rather than optional add-ons.

'Assessment support' should generate implementation evidence from the beginning through lightweight but systematic signals such as pre/post prompts, participation traces, and tagged artifacts, since otherwise the pilot cannot inform scaling decisions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly agree to design 'a small pilot' for Ways of Knowing.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the pilot is testing the academic proposition: whether a first-year cluster built around shared interdisciplinary questions, common writing, and a few coordinated moments produces worthwhile integrative learning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the pilot is testing the delivery proposition: whether a deliberately designed student journey with onboarding, cross-course prompts, digital continuity, and support touchpoints can make interdisciplinarity legible and scalable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both hear 'small pilot' as prudent and fundable, and both imagine one cohort in one semester; the divergence lies in the object of experimentation rather than its size, which feels too implicit to surface during brainstorming.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss building the concept around 'interdisciplinary team teaching' inspired by the chapter themes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses the phrase to mean faculty from different disciplines visibly intersecting through guest-teaching in one another's classes, co-framed assignments, and perhaps a kickoff or showcase session, while each retains primary control of their own course meetings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses the phrase to mean a recurring co-facilitated student experience in which both instructors are jointly present in the same teaching session often enough for students to see disciplines actively negotiating ideas together.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because they are brainstorming pedagogy rather than discussing teaching loads, both can use 'interdisciplinary team teaching' sincerely without triggering logistics; each version sounds aligned with the book’s spirit and with common campus rhetoric.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that a learning-community model could be the right frame for the first-year experience.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the learning community consists of linked enrollment across two existing courses, a common inquiry thread, and a handful of shared academic events such as a speaker, panel, or end-of-term showcase.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the learning community also includes non-course structures that students experience continuously, such as peer mentors, a brief advising cadence, and a persistent online space for cross-course dialogue and portfolio work.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term already has institutional legitimacy and broad positive connotations, so each maps it onto a familiar model from prior work; the mismatch concerns the edges of what is naturally included, not the recognizable core.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include 'assessment support' so the concept note appears responsible and evidence-based.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes assessment support means a common integrative-thinking rubric, a curated sample of student essays or portfolios, and a faculty debrief at the end of the semester.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes assessment support means setting up lightweight pre/post prompts, LMS or platform traces, artifact tagging, and a simple evaluation workflow that documents how students moved through the designed experience.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are comfortable signaling that the project will be assessed, and at concept-note stage the phrase remains abstract enough to carry different implementation models without friction; neither sees a reason to unpack the methods yet.

turns.inner_thought: The chapter headings give us exactly the kind of respectable language faculty governance likes: interdisciplinarity, writing, learning communities, assessment. If I keep this framed as a small pilot for next spring, everyone will hear prudence. What I need is permission to test the academic idea in a contained form using existing courses, not an expectation that we build a whole support ecosystem around it.
turns.utterance: I keep thinking the chapter themes point toward a really compelling first-year concept for Ways of Knowing. If we’re careful, we could shape a small pilot the university would be comfortable backing next spring.

turns.inner_thought: Small is good as long as it still counts as a real test of the student-facing model. Central funders will want to see something students can actually move through, not just a nice intellectual premise. I should keep it sounding manageable and distinctive without naming too much of the machinery yet.
turns.utterance: I think so too. A small pilot gives us a manageable way to try it, and it still makes room for the proposal to feel distinctive enough for central funding.

turns.inner_thought: The cleanest version is two existing courses, probably humanities and science, linked by a broad question and one shared writing sequence. If we call that interdisciplinary team teaching, people will picture serious collaboration, while I can still preserve normal course ownership and staffing.
turns.utterance: One promising shape would be to build it around interdisciplinary team teaching—maybe pairing a humanities seminar with an introductory science course around a shared question and a common writing task.

turns.inner_thought: That pairing works, but for interdisciplinary team teaching to be credible from a design standpoint, students need to witness the disciplines interacting more than just symbolically. I can cue that by talking about visibility and recurring moments, without getting concrete enough to trigger a workload debate.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think that could be especially strong if interdisciplinary team teaching is something students can really see happening at key moments across the term.

turns.inner_thought: Learning-community language gives this institutional legitimacy. For me that means linked enrollment, coordinated inquiry, and a couple of shared academic occasions—enough to create coherence without adding separate structures that departments would have to service.
turns.utterance: A learning-community model could be the right frame for the first-year experience. I’m imagining linked enrollment and a few shared moments so the whole thing feels coherent rather than just adjacent.

turns.inner_thought: Good. In my mind the learning community needs continuous structures students actually feel: a digital home, peer mentoring, light advising, recurring cross-course touchpoints. But I should keep that bundled under softer language so it still sounds light and natural to her.
turns.utterance: I agree—the learning-community frame helps a lot. We could build in some continuous touchpoints so students have a clearer sense of connection across the experience.

turns.inner_thought: Integrative writing is the safest center of gravity. If we layer prompts onto existing syllabi, we can test whether the academic proposition works without asking faculty to rebuild courses or surrender autonomy. That keeps the pilot elegant and staffable.
turns.utterance: To keep it focused, I’d be inclined to have the small pilot revolve around a sequence of integrative writing prompts layered onto existing syllabi, so we’re not redesigning whole courses.

turns.inner_thought: That’s exactly the kind of content spine I can wrap a coherent student journey around. I’m thinking entry point, recurring cross-course moments, and a simple flow for students to carry work forward, but I need to keep it abstract so she hears coherence rather than infrastructure.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Those prompts could give the small pilot a visible throughline, so the different pieces read to students as one experience rather than isolated assignments.

turns.inner_thought: We definitely need assessment support in the concept note, but I want it to sound conventional and faculty-friendly: shared rubric, sample artifacts, end-of-term review. Enough evidence to satisfy reviewers, nothing that looks like an extra compliance apparatus.
turns.utterance: And I do think we should explicitly include assessment support so the note reads as responsible and evidence-based, but in a way that stays pretty straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: Yes—assessment support also needs to tell us how the implementation worked, not just whether a few final papers looked good. I’m imagining lightweight baseline and end signals, some traces from the platform, and tagged artifacts, but I’ll present it as minimal learning data so it doesn’t sound overbuilt.
turns.utterance: Agreed on assessment support. We can probably gather a few lightweight signals along the way as well, just enough to learn from the pilot without making it feel overengineered.

turns.inner_thought: A cohort of twenty keeps this politically safe. If departments hear academically elegant, easy to adopt, and respectful of faculty control, they may actually volunteer. The phrase interdisciplinary team teaching can do a lot of rhetorical work here without forcing full co-teaching commitments.
turns.utterance: I’d keep the first cohort to around twenty students. If we present it as academically elegant and easy for faculty to adopt, I think departments will be much more open to participating.

turns.inner_thought: Twenty is enough to prototype a real model. I want the concept note to imply replicability: a learning-community pilot with a clear arc and implementation logic that central leadership can imagine scaling. I’ll keep the phrasing broad so it sounds supportive, not bureaucratic.
turns.utterance: That scale feels right to me. We could package it as a replicable learning-community pilot, with a concise implementation frame so people can immediately see how it would work.

turns.inner_thought: This is the right summary: learning community, interdisciplinary team teaching, integrative writing, assessment support. That gives me enough to draft an academic rationale faculty will trust, and I can keep the note anchored in curricular credibility rather than operational ambition.
turns.utterance: So the way I’m hearing it, we have a learning-community pilot built around interdisciplinary team teaching, integrative writing, and assessment support. If that sounds right, I’m happy to draft the academic rationale.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. She’ll make it academically legitimate; I’ll make it look like a coherent student experience with enough structure to win funding and inform scaling. As long as we merge those pieces cleanly, this can read as a flagship pilot.
turns.utterance: That sounds right. I’ll draft the pilot structure, the student-facing flow, and the support side, and then we can merge our pieces into one concept note by Friday.
